title: The Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:1–18)
hook: the people sing; the rabbis say God hushed the angels because the Egyptians were drowning (Megillah 10b)

segments.voice: Yesterday, at the sea: an army behind, water ahead, and Nachshon walking in up to his nose. Your line was walk in first. Did you take a first step? Now they're on the other side. Day ninety.

A test result that comes back clear. A phone call saying they're safe. The moment the thing chasing you is gone. Relief like that, multiplied by a whole people, standing on a beach at dawn, soaking wet, looking back at the water where the army was. Generations of slavery, and it's over. What do you do in a moment like that? They sing. Today: the song, and the angels who weren't allowed to join in.
screen: `A TEST RESULT THAT COMES BACK CLEAR.` → `A PEOPLE ON A BEACH AT DAWN.` → `THEY SING.`

segments.voice: "Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD." And the song begins: "I will sing unto the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea." It's called Shirat HaYam, the Song of the Sea. In a Torah scroll it's even written differently from the text around it, laid out in a pattern like bricks in a wall. And one line from it, "Who is like unto Thee, O LORD, among the mighty?" in Hebrew mi chamocha, is said in Jewish prayer every single day. So the song is honored. Nobody tells the people they were wrong to sing. But the Talmud tells a story about that same moment. Up in heaven, it says, the ministering angels wanted to sing too. And God stopped them. The works of my hands are drowning in the sea, and you want to sing? The Egyptians were enemies. They'd enslaved and chased the Israelites. And they were still God's creatures. The Talmud adds a subtle line: God doesn't rejoice at the downfall of the wicked, though God may let others rejoice. The people who were just saved can sing. But nobody should throw a party over someone drowning. In the same spirit, at the seder, when the ten plagues are read, many people spill a drop of wine for each one. One explanation: a full cup is a sign of joy, and the joy is made a little less, because people suffered. The book of Proverbs says it too: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth." You can be grateful you're safe. You can sing. Just don't sing over the drowning.
screen: `I WILL SING UNTO THE LORD.` · `MI CHAMOCHA, EVERY DAY.` · `GOD HUSHES THE ANGELS.` · `A DROP OF WINE FOR EACH PLAGUE.` · then, large: `REJOICE NOT WHEN THINE ENEMY FALLETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: celebrate without gloating. Settle, and breathe. Think of a recent win. Something that went your way: an argument you won, a game, a promotion, a rival who stumbled. Let yourself be glad about it. Really glad. Then think of the person on the other side. What did it cost them? Hold both at once, the joy and the other person. If you pray, you can give thanks for what went well. The bell holds the time.
The Song of the Sea. Shirat HaYam. The people's song of thanks on the far shore, sung while the angels were told to be quiet.
screen: `THE SONG OF THE SEA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: don't sing over the drowning. Today, when something goes your way, enjoy it, and be kind to whoever it didn't go well for. Day ninety.

howItsDone: Jews say the Song of the Sea in the morning prayers, and its line mi chamocha in the evening and morning prayers; at the seder many spill a drop of wine for each plague, and the Song is read in synagogue on the seventh day of Passover.

options: God stopped them: my creatures are drowning.
the angels sang a sad song instead.
fork.reveal: God said: the works of my hands are drowning in the sea, and you would sing? the people's thanks stands; the angels stay silent.

original.note: Hebrew: who is like You? a line from the Song, said in Jewish prayer every day.

trapdoor: what you thought: a victory song over a defeated enemy.
what it means: a song of thanks from people who were saved, while even heaven is told not to celebrate the drowning.
what a scholar hears: Megillah 10b and Sanhedrin 39b: God hushes the angels; he does not rejoice, but lets others rejoice. the scroll's brick layout is set out in Megillah 16b.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Exodus 15:1 ('for He is highly exalted'), 15:11, and Proverbs 24:17.
Megillah 10b / Sanhedrin 39b paraphrased, including Rabbi Elazar's nuance ('He does not rejoice, but causes others to rejoice'). Confirm.
The wine-drop custom's meaning (diminished joy) is widely taught but its origin is medieval and explanations vary. Confirm framing.
Brick-pattern layout of the Song in the scroll (ariach al gabei leveinah), Megillah 16b. Confirm.
Mi chamocha in daily prayer (after the Shema, morning and evening): confirm.

Reviewer edit: 'four hundred years of slavery' softened to 'generations of slavery'; the length is debated (Genesis 15:13 says 400 years of affliction, Exodus 12:40 says 430 years in Egypt, rabbinic reckoning gives 210 years in Egypt). 'One of the oldest poems' softened to 'many scholars count among the oldest'; the dating is academic and debated. 'That's why' link between Megillah 10b and the seder wine drops softened to 'in the same spirit', since the custom is later and its explanations vary.

Editor review: banned opener 'Think of' and 'the biggest relief you've ever felt' removed from hook and screen; 'many scholars count among the oldest poems' cut (claims rule); the wine-drop meaning is now 'one explanation'.
